rulesSummary.title: How to play
rulesSummary.intro: Build seven rival companies across a shared grid and profit from the stock you hold in them. Everyone starts with ${cash} and a rack of {hand} tiles. The richest player when the game ends wins.

turn.heading: A turn
turn.place: **Place a tile.** A lone tile does nothing. Next to loose tiles it *founds* a company — you pick which of the free companies to raise and take one free share. Next to one company it *grows* that company. Between two or more, it *merges* them.
turn.buy: **Buy stock** — up to {max} shares in any active companies, if you can afford them and the bank still has them.
turn.note: A company that reaches its “safe” size can never be dissolved. Once a company is safe, or the largest company passes the end-size, any player may call the game on their turn. Under the Boomtown set a player may instead put the ending to a vote before that point — see *going public* below.

mergers.heading: Mergers
mergers.intro: The larger company survives and swallows the smaller; you break ties. The placed tile is set aside while sizes, prices and bonuses are worked out, then joins the survivor. For each dissolved company, largest first:
mergers.bonus: its shareholders are paid a bonus, scaled to the company’s size just before the merger — biggest holder gets the most;
mergers.disposal: then, starting with whoever caused the merger and going clockwise, each holder may keep their now-defunct shares, sell them to the bank, or trade two of them for one share of the survivor.
mergers.note: A dissolved company’s headquarters returns to the tray. If that company is founded again later, like a zombie rising from the dead, the shares you kept come back to life with it.

goingPublic.heading: Going public — the Boomtown set only
goingPublic.body: The books are closed: your cash and holdings are private. Once {quorum} companies are safe, any player may end their turn by moving to liquidate. That publishes the register — one vote per share held in a safe company — and everyone votes in turn. It carries on {quotaFour}% of the register — {quotaSix}% at five players or more — with at least {backers} players behind it, and the game ends immediately.
goingPublic.note: Backing a motion that fails costs you your privacy: every backer plays the rest of the game with their books open. Voting against costs nothing. One motion each, all game.

comparison.heading: Where the rule sets differ
comparison.twoPlayerBank: the bank holds shares too, drawn fresh each merger
comparison.twoPlayerNoVote: played straight — but no vote under {n} players

rulesSummary.footNote: Boomtown is the default: Classic with the books closed and the ending put to a vote — our own variant rather than a published one, and it comes alive at three players or more. The other two are reconstructions, there for a table that wants the published rules; cash and price both climb faster in the Modern set, and Classic runs a little longer.

turn.title: Your turn, in order
turn.place: **Place a tile.** Mandatory if any tile in hand can be played. It either sits alone, *founds* a corporation (pick any free headquarters and take a free share), *grows* the one corporation it touches, or *merges* two or more.
turn.buy: **Buy stock.** Optional — up to {max} shares in any corporations already on the board, as far as your cash and the bank's stock allow.
turn.draw: **Draw back to {hand}.** A tile that could never be played — one that would merge two safe corporations — {deadTile}
turn.deadTileDiscard: is turned face up, set out of play, and replaced.
turn.end: **Call the end, or don't.** Once a corporation reaches {endSize} tiles you *may* end the game. Never forced.
turn.endVote: Before that point you may instead *move to liquidate* and put the ending to a vote — see **Going Public**.

merger.title: When corporations merge
merger.note: The only part of the game where order really matters. The tile you just placed **never counts** toward either corporation — not for size, price or bonuses. It joins the survivor once the dust settles.
merger.survivor: **Biggest survives.** On a tie the player who placed the tile chooses. A corporation of {safe} tiles or more is safe and can never be dissolved — so two safe corporations can never merge at all.
merger.order: **Defunct chains resolve one at a time, largest first**, each finished before the next begins.
merger.bonuses: **Bonuses are paid** to its largest shareholders — {tiers} — priced at the size it was *before* the merger. Nothing is paid on the survivor.
merger.disposal: **Then everyone disposes of the dead stock**, starting with the player who placed the tile and going clockwise. Each of you splits your shares however you like between *holding* them, *selling* at the defunct price, and *trading* two of them for one share of the survivor.
merger.headquarters: **The headquarters goes back to the tray.** That name can be founded again later — and, like a zombie rising from the dead, any shares you kept come back to life with it.

goingPublic.title: Going public: the alternate ending
goingPublic.note: Nobody has to wait for one enormous corporation: a vote can be called to end the game early, and the table decides.
goingPublic.window: **The window opens** once {quorum} corporations are safe. It closes again the moment the game could simply be ended the ordinary way — asking is pointless when one mega-corporation can simply announce the end.
goingPublic.moving: **Any player, at the end of their own turn, may move to liquidate** — {allowance}. Motioning for a vote *is* voting for it; you cannot propose an ending and then vote it down.
goingPublic.register: **The register is published** the first time anyone moves, and stays public for the rest of the game. It is one vote per share held in a *safe* corporation — those are the only companies certain to still exist at settlement. *Stock in a chain that can still be eaten carries no vote.*
goingPublic.voting: **Everyone votes in turn**, starting with the mover and going clockwise. It carries on {quota}% of the register with at least {backers} players behind it, and the game ends there and then. Settling now pays everyone out at once.
goingPublic.price: **If it fails, everyone who backed it opens their books** — cash and holdings visible to the table for the rest of the game. That is the whole price of a yes: voting against costs nothing, so a speculative or spiteful motion is expensive and a sincere one is nearly free.
goingPublic.standing: Calling a vote to go public is a *high risk, high reward* move. Read the table shrewdly and it can be a game-changer, read it wrong and it can spell disaster.

worthKnowing.title: Worth knowing
worthKnowing.closedBooks: **The books are closed.** Cash and holdings are private — yours alone, and this rule set fixes it that way. What anyone owns has to be inferred from what they have been seen to buy, so a purchase is a statement as much as an investment.
worthKnowing.finiteStock: **Stock is finite.** An empty bank blocks buying, the founder's free share and 2-for-1 trades alike.
worthKnowing.noSelling: **Shares don't sell on demand.** Stock only becomes cash in a merger or in the final settlement.
worthKnowing.broke: **Being broke is playable.** With no cash you still place and draw. Nobody is knocked out.
worthKnowing.safe: **Safe is permanent** — and a safe corporation still grows and still swallows others.
worthKnowing.settlement: **At the end**, every corporation still standing pays bonuses as if it were merging, then the bank buys back all stock at its current price. Shares in a corporation that never made it onto the board are worth nothing.
